entries.clue: Some disrupt a keynoter's understanding (6)

indicatorNotes.Some: Some of a thing is a part of it taken as it comes, so the letters wanted sit together inside the words that follow.

blocks.note: six letters in a row starting three into the first word, running straight across two spaces

annotation.surface: A few people in the audience wrecking the keynote speaker's grasp of things.
annotation.walkthrough: Uptake survives in ordinary speech almost only in 'quick on the uptake', which is where this sense comes from. Two word breaks and an apostrophe fall inside the run, and the eye slides over joins like those.
annotation.definitionFit: To be quick on the uptake is to be quick to understand, so uptake is the taking-in of meaning itself.

entries.clue: China grows; upper bounds showing value of money (10,5)

indicatorNotes.bounds: To bound is to leap, and letters that go leaping do not come down in the order they set off in.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, fifteen letters across three words, the semicolon counting for nothing
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: China's economy expanding, with its upper limits showing what money is really worth.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Upper bounds' is a phrase out of mathematics, and phrases like that are built to look like part of the sentence rather than an instruction sitting inside it. Fifteen letters is the longest fodder a grid this size can take.
annotation.definitionFit: Purchasing power is how much a unit of currency will actually buy, which is the value of money rather than the figure printed on it.

entries.clue: Street paved with gold bearing up somewhere in C Europe (7)

indicatorNotes.paved with: Paving is laid into a road rather than beside it, so what the street is paved with closes round the street itself.
indicatorNotes.up: In a down entry up runs against the way the letters are written, so the piece is read from its last letter back to its first.

blocks.note: au is gold's chemical symbol, from the Latin aurum
st = street, as written on any address
a person's bearing is their air, and in a down entry it is read upwards

annotation.surface: The proverbial street paved with gold, holding up somewhere in central Europe.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Gold bearing' wants to be read as one thing, the way gold-bearing rock is, and the two words belong to different pieces. A bearing is the air a person carries themselves with. C is the setter's shorthand for central.
annotation.definitionFit: Austria is the landlocked republic in the middle of Europe, one of the places the loose 'somewhere in C Europe' can be pointing at.

entries.clue: I'm alone, to regrettably become het up (9)

indicatorNotes.regrettably: What is regrettable has gone wrong, and letters gone wrong are letters no longer in the order they should be.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, nine letters, the apostrophe counting for nothing
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: Someone left on their own and working themselves up about it.
annotation.walkthrough: Het up is 'heated up' worn down by use, and it survives only in that phrase. The split infinitive — 'to regrettably become' — is clumsy English, and clumsiness in a clue usually marks an instruction in disguise.
annotation.definitionFit: Somebody het up is worked up and running on feeling rather than thought, which is what being emotional amounts to.

entries.clue: After reflection, stop accommodating 51 aviators (6)

indicatorNotes.After reflection: A reflection hands back what faces it the other way round, so the letters built up are read back to front.
indicatorNotes.accommodating: To accommodate someone is to take them in and give them room, so those letters go inside rather than alongside.

blocks.note: the clue's own word, which opens up before its last letter
51 in Roman figures: L is fifty and I is one

annotation.surface: Somebody thinking better of it and refusing to put up fifty-one airmen.
annotation.walkthrough: 'After reflection' reads as second thoughts and is an instruction to read the letters backwards. Roman figures are the crossword's usual way of turning a number into letters, and 51 has only the one spelling.
annotation.definitionFit: Aviators are the people who fly aircraft, which is a pilot's trade.

entries.clue: What may follow cut meat prepared for sandwiches? (5)

blocks.note: the second half of the pair of commands every computer offers for shifting a block of text about
the potted meat spread sold in small British jars and put straight on the bread

annotation.surface: A question about what comes next once the meat for the sandwiches has been cut.
annotation.walkthrough: The word cut does two jobs at once: it closes the first definition and it opens the surface's cut meat. Meat paste is a British larder staple — potted beef, salmon and shrimp — sold in the same little jars it was a century ago.
annotation.definitionFit: Paste is the second half of the computer pair cut and paste, and meat paste is the potted spread made for sandwiches.

entries.clue: Location encompassing Beirut, a nation - originally Natufian, primarily? (7)

annotation.definition: Location encompassing Beirut, a nation - originally Natufian, primarily?

indicatorNotes.primarily: What is primary comes first, so each word gives up only the letter it begins with.

blocks.clueFragment: Location encompassing Beirut, a nation - originally Natufian
blocks.note: the opening letters of the seven words, taken in the order they are written

annotation.surface: A place that takes in Beirut, and a nation whose earliest people were the Natufians.
annotation.walkthrough: Every word does double duty: the sentence describes the country and the same words hand over their initials. The Natufians were the hunter-gatherers of the Levant twelve thousand years ago, the first people there known to have stayed put.
annotation.definitionFit: Read straight, the clue is the country itself: the Mediterranean state Beirut is capital of, on the Levantine ground where Natufian culture began.

entries.clue: Midnight: time with which cat may be familiar (3,8,4)

annotation.definition2: time with which cat may be familiar

blocks.note: the hour at which the night is held to turn and the dark business of the small hours begins

blocks.clueFragment: time with which cat may be familiar
blocks.note: a familiar is the animal spirit that attends a witch, most often a black cat, and this is its working hour

annotation.surface: A cat that knows exactly what time it is in the middle of the night.
annotation.walkthrough: Familiar is the hinge: as an adjective it means well acquainted, as a noun it is the creature that serves a witch. The phrase comes down from Hamlet — ''tis now the very witching time of night'.
annotation.definitionFit: The witching hour is midnight, when witches were said to be abroad, and a witch's familiar is traditionally a cat.

entries.clue: Sober - to blame? (11)

blocks.note: steady and serious, the sort of person you would leave in charge
whoever is to blame is the one the fault is laid at the door of

annotation.surface: Asking whether the sober one is the one at fault.
annotation.walkthrough: The dash does the work of a question mark, setting two senses side by side with nothing else to go on. Sober here means level-headed rather than off the drink, and the drink is what the surface offers instead.
annotation.definitionFit: A responsible person is steady and dependable, which is sober in its serious sense, and to be responsible for a mess is to be to blame for it.

entries.clue: Grasp where your luggage will be stowed? (4)

annotation.definition2: where your luggage will be stowed

blocks.note: to have something gripped and not let it go

blocks.clueFragment: where your luggage will be stowed
blocks.note: the cargo space below a ship's deck, or the one under an aircraft cabin, that the cases go into

annotation.surface: Being told to get your head round where the bags end up.
annotation.walkthrough: Grasp reads as understand, a third sense the clue never needs — it wants the plain physical grip. On a ship the hold is the space below decks the cargo goes into, and an aircraft's is under the cabin floor.
annotation.definitionFit: To grasp a thing is to have hold of it, and a ship's or plane's hold is the compartment luggage is stowed in.

entries.clue: Footballer's games destroying Blues regularly (4)

indicatorNotes.regularly: Regularly means at an even interval, so the word is worked through at every other step instead of letter by letter.

blocks.note: pe is physical education, the games lesson on a school timetable
every other letter of Blues is struck out — the B, the U and the S — and this pair is left standing

annotation.surface: A footballer whose matches take Chelsea apart week after week.
annotation.walkthrough: The Blues is the nickname of Chelsea and of Birmingham City, which is what keeps the surface on a football pitch. Pelé got the name as a boy, disliked it, and never found out what it meant.
annotation.definitionFit: Pelé is the Brazilian forward who won three World Cups and is the footballer most often named the greatest of them all.

entries.clue: Failing that is here to - initially - worry about (9)

indicatorNotes.initially: Initially means at the outset, so the word hands over only the letter it begins with.
indicatorNotes.about: Something shifted about finishes somewhere other than where it started, and letters shifted about land in a new order.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, eight letters across three words
the letter worry starts with, the ninth the answer needs
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: A shortcoming sitting right here, the first thing anybody need worry about.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Failing that' reads in the surface as a noun and a pronoun, where the failing is a fault. The dashes round 'initially' look like an aside and are the only sign that a single letter is wanted.
annotation.definitionFit: Otherwise means if that does not come off, which is the job 'failing that' does when it introduces the fallback.

entries.clue: Green Day's forerunner approaching, did you say? (5)

indicatorNotes.did you say: Asking what you said points at how the words come out of the mouth rather than at how they are spelt.

blocks.note: the eve runs ahead of the day it belongs to, as Christmas Eve does, and whatever is approaching is nigh; the adjective is spoken in front of its noun

annotation.surface: Somebody asking whether the night before the big day is nearly upon us.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Green Day' looks like the band, and the group has nothing to do with it: Green is the definition standing alone and Day belongs to the wordplay. The adjective is said first though it is written last.
annotation.definitionFit: Green describes somebody raw and easily taken in, the same green as in greenhorn, which is what being naive is.

entries.clue: Amid clamour, retro ads I scorn (7)

indicatorNotes.Amid: To be amid something is to be in the middle of it, so the letters named next sit inside the word that follows.
indicatorNotes.retro: Retro looks backwards, so the letters it covers are taken in the reverse of the order they are written.

blocks.note: a din is a clamour, and it opens up after its first letter
the three letters of ads and the single I, read the other way round

annotation.surface: In all the racket, the vintage advertisements are the ones I look down on.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Retro ads' reads as vintage advertising, which is exactly the cover wanted — retro is the instruction, not a description of the ads. A din is the crossword's shortest word for noise and turns up whenever three letters are needed.
annotation.definitionFit: To disdain a thing is to hold it beneath you and say so, which is what it is to scorn it.

entries.clue: Horned god with hunger to demonstrate swagger (7)

blocks.note: Pan is the goat-legged, horned god of the Greek wild, the one whose name is in panic
to ache for something is to hunger for it

annotation.surface: A horned god with an appetite, out to make a display of himself.
annotation.walkthrough: Panache began as the plume on a helmet, which is why it still means a flourish you can see rather than quiet confidence. Pan is the crossword's usual horned god, and the shortest one going.
annotation.definitionFit: Swagger is doing a thing with visible style and self-assurance, which is exactly what doing it with panache means.

entries.clue: Depicted as predatory savage (9)

indicatorNotes.savage: To savage something is to tear into it and leave it in pieces, and letters left in pieces are letters out of order.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, nine letters
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: Somebody painted as a predatory brute.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Predatory savage' reads as one noun phrase, so the word doing the shuffling looks like part of what is being described. Every letter comes out of the single word before it, with nothing joined in from elsewhere.
annotation.definitionFit: To portray someone is to set them down in a picture or a description, which is to depict them.

entries.clue: Doc charged with ear, nose and throat: hospital's left decongestant (7)

indicatorNotes.charged with: To be charged with something is to have it put into your keeping, so those letters end up inside the word before them.

blocks.note: an MO is a medical officer, the doctor attached to a unit or a ship, and it opens up after its first letter
ENT is what the hospital department is called on the signs
h = hospital, the letter on the road sign
l = left, the standard shorthand

annotation.surface: A doctor answering for ear, nose and throat, and all the hospital has left is a decongestant.
annotation.walkthrough: The medical surface is doing the hiding: every word of it belongs in a hospital, so not one of them stands out as an instruction. Menthol comes from mint oil and works by tricking the nerves into reporting cold.
annotation.definitionFit: Menthol is the cooling compound from mint oil that goes into rubs and lozenges to clear a blocked nose.

entries.clue: Sulking, Everyman's taking on work (4)

indicatorNotes.taking on: To take something on is to take it aboard and carry it, so the letters named next travel inside.

blocks.note: Everyman writes himself into his own clues in the first person, so what is Everyman's is my own; it opens up after its first letter
op is opus, a composer's numbered work

annotation.surface: Everyman grudgingly accepting another job.
annotation.walkthrough: Everyman signs himself into the wordplay whenever his name appears, and it always means the first person — here the possessive form of it. Mopy is the adjective from mope, and the dictionaries spell it without an e.
annotation.definitionFit: Someone mopy is low and listless and will not be cheered up, which is what sulking looks like from outside.

entries.clue: Like uplands - welcoming sherpa thither, ultimately - that's me (7)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition is not a synonym but the man speaking: the whole clue is put in the first person, so 'that's me' is Sir Edmund introducing himself.

indicatorNotes.welcoming: To welcome someone is to take them in, so those letters go inside the word before them.
indicatorNotes.ultimately: Ultimately means at the very end, so each word gives up only the letter it finishes on.

blocks.note: ground like uplands is hilly, and the word opens up before its last letter
the closing letters of the two words, taken in that order

annotation.surface: A man who says he is like the high country, and made a sherpa welcome up there.
annotation.walkthrough: Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay, a Sherpa, stood on the summit of Everest together in 1953, which is why a sherpa is the company the clue gives him. 'Thither' means to that place, and it is there for its last letter alone.
annotation.definitionFit: Sir Edmund Hillary, the New Zealander who with Tenzing Norgay first reached the top of Everest, is the man speaking the clue.

entries.clue: Carries, and plays 'donkey' game again? (7)

blocks.note: re- is the prefix English hangs on a verb to mean once more
the party game is pin the tail on the donkey, so whoever plays it tails the creature

annotation.surface: Somebody who takes the load and has another go at pin the tail on the donkey.
annotation.walkthrough: A shop carries a line when it stocks it and sells it on, and that trade sense is the one the definition wants. The quotation marks round 'donkey' mark it as a name out of a game rather than the animal.
annotation.definitionFit: A shop that retails a product carries it — keeps it on the shelves and sells it on — which is the trade sense of carrying a line.

entries.clue: I butter up, presenting ode? (7)

indicatorNotes.up: Up in the sense of upset: what is up is no longer lying as it was, and letters no longer lying as they were are in a new order.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, seven letters
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: A flatterer admitting they lay it on thick, and handing over a poem to prove it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Butter up' is the phrasal verb for flattering, and the clue splits it down the middle: the butter is raw material and the up is the instruction. The question mark concedes that a poem of praise is only one kind of the thing.
annotation.definitionFit: An ode is a poem written in praise of someone or something, which is one of the forms a tribute takes.

entries.clue: Part of eye raised to access virtual assistant (4)

indicatorNotes.raised: In a down entry a raised word is lifted back up the column, so its letters are read from the bottom to the top.

blocks.note: the coloured ring round the pupil is the iris, here read upwards

annotation.surface: Raising part of the eye as the way to get at a phone's helper.
annotation.walkthrough: Iris is the crossword's favourite part of the eye because it is a flower and a Greek goddess as well; here it is only the eye. Siri arrived with the iPhone 4S in 2011 and the name is Norwegian.
annotation.definitionFit: Siri is the voice assistant built into Apple's phones and computers, an assistant with no body to it.

entries.clue: Heard in Australia: folk related to His Holiness (5)

indicatorNotes.Heard in Australia: Heard points at the sound of the word rather than its spelling, and in Australia names the accent it is to be said in.

blocks.note: folk are people, and in a broad Australian mouth the vowels flatten until the two syllables come out as these five letters

annotation.surface: Australians who turn out to be relatives of the Pope.
annotation.walkthrough: His Holiness is how the Pope is addressed, so the word wanted is the adjective for his office. The accent has to be laid on very thick indeed: solvers in Sydney wrote in to say no Australian says it this way.
annotation.definitionFit: His Holiness is the Pope's formal style, and papal is the adjective for anything belonging to the Pope or his office.

entries.clue: Cut off heavy drinker, perhaps it's a sign (9)

indicatorNotes.Cut off: To cut something off is to take its end away, so the word turns up without the letter it finished on.

blocks.note: heavy is hard, and cutting it off loses the D it ends on
a binger is somebody who goes on a binge, which is one sort of drinker among many

annotation.surface: A heavy drinker cut off at the bar, which may be a sign of something.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cut off' reads as what a barman does to a customer who has had enough, and it is an instruction to lose a letter. The word once meant the man sent ahead of an army to find it lodgings.
annotation.definitionFit: A harbinger is whatever arrives first and announces what is coming behind it, so it is a sign of something on its way.

entries.clue: Guard stall (5)

blocks.note: the betting sense: backing the other outcome too, so that nothing can be lost whichever way it goes
answering a question in a way that commits to nothing, to put off the moment of saying

annotation.surface: An instruction to keep watch over the market stall.
annotation.walkthrough: Both words are verbs here, and the row of garden shrubs is the sense neither of them wants. Hedging a bet and hedging a question are the same move made in two different rooms.
annotation.definitionFit: To hedge a bet is to guard against loss by covering both outcomes, and to hedge a question is to stall instead of answering it.

entries.clue: Concerning situation, monarch's demand? (4,2,3,2)

annotation.definitionNote: Neither half is a synonym, because the answer is a spoken question; each definition names the occasion that prompts it instead.

blocks.note: the helpless question you put when the state of things is worrying and nothing can be done about it
the enquiry royalty is famous for making of every person presented at a walkabout or an investiture

annotation.surface: A king making demands about a worrying state of affairs.
annotation.walkthrough: The question is the one the late Queen was known for in a receiving line, put to each person in turn. Read the other way it is the shrug you give at a situation there is no answer to.
annotation.definitionFit: 'What do you do?' is both the shrug at a situation nothing can be done about and the stock question a royal puts to a stranger.

entries.clue: Lethargy! Lethargic to some extent, seeing pattern on socks (6)

indicatorNotes.to some extent: To some extent is part of the way rather than all of it, so only a stretch of the words is wanted, taken unbroken.

blocks.note: six letters in a row from the fourth of the first word, running straight through the exclamation mark and the space

annotation.surface: Sheer tiredness, brought on in part by the sight of those socks.
annotation.walkthrough: Repeating a word in two forms lets the setter lay a long run of letters across a join the eye will not stop at. The diamond knit is named for Argyll in western Scotland, and comes from the tartan of the Campbells.
annotation.definitionFit: Argyle is the diamond-and-overstripe knit that golfers' and schoolboys' socks are patterned with, named from the Scottish district of Argyll.

entries.clue: Unexciting bottom entertained in course of empty day (6)

indicatorNotes.entertained in course of: To entertain a guest in the course of a day is to have them inside it, so those letters sit within the word that follows.
indicatorNotes.empty: An emptied word keeps its walls and loses everything between them, so only the letters at the two ends survive.

blocks.note: day with its middle taken out, leaving the letters at either end
the rear of anything is its bottom end

annotation.surface: Dull company being kept amused through the course of a day with nothing in it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Empty' is the instruction, and it hides inside a phrase anybody would write without thinking — an empty day. Bottom is the nursery word for the rear, not the bottom of a page or a hill.
annotation.definitionFit: Something dreary is grey and dull and holds out nothing to look forward to, which is as unexciting as it gets.
